# THE DEAD SPOT

## A Novel

---

# PART ONE: THE INBOUND PASS

---

## Chapter 1

The gym smelled wrong.

Dez Okafor noticed this before she noticed anything else, before the lights that shouldn't have been on, before the wheelchair lying on its side near the bleachers with one push rim still rotating in some impossible physics of aftermath. The gym smelled like copper and floor wax and, beneath those, something chemical—sharp and sweet together, the way a thing smells when it's trying not to smell like anything at all.

It was 5:47 a.m. on a Wednesday, and Dez was early because Dez was always early, because the only time the court belonged entirely to her was before anyone else's alarm had gone off. She'd transferred from her everyday chair to her sport chair in the parking lot, the December air biting her bare arms, and she'd wheeled through the side entrance that Ray always left unlocked for her. That had been their secret, hers and Ray's. Every morning since September. The unlocked door, the dark gym, the hour of solitude before the world filled up with other people's voices.

But the lights were on.

And Ray Pulaski was lying face-down on the baseline, under the far basket, in a position that looked, for one absurd and merciful half-second, like he'd fallen asleep doing push-ups.

Dez did not scream. She would think about that later, would turn it over in her mind like a stone she'd found on a beach—the fact that she had not screamed. She had stopped her chair at half-court, and her hands had gone still on the push rims, and she had looked. That was all. She had looked, and the gymnasium had looked back, enormous and silent and flooded with its wrong fluorescent light, and the information had entered her body all at once: his stillness, the color of the floor around him, the absolute zero of his breathing.

She called 911 at 5:48. Her voice, on the recording that would later be played in several rooms she'd never seen, was flat and precise, the voice of a sixteen-year-old girl reporting coordinates in a war.

---

Raymond James Pulaski was fifty-one years old and had been the equipment manager for the Eastlake Academy Wheelhawks for eleven seasons. He was a large, slope-shouldered man who wore the same rotation of four polo shirts, each embroidered with the Eastlake crest, and who knew the tire pressure preference of every player who'd ever rolled through his gym. He called everyone "chief." He had a dog named Bonkers and an ex-wife in Tampa and a storage unit full of VHS tapes that no one, in the coming investigation, would think to look at for almost three days.

He had been struck on the back of the head with a blunt object that was never found, and he had fallen, and the fall had not killed him. What killed him, the medical examiner would determine, was the subsequent compression of his airway against the hardwood while he lay unconscious, face-down, in the manner of a man who'd fallen asleep doing push-ups. Someone had pressed down on the back of his neck. Someone had waited. The bruising suggested gloved hands—not leather, the examiner would note, but something thinner. Latex, perhaps. Nitrile. The kind of gloves you'd find in a first-aid kit.

The kind of gloves kept in the equipment cage.

---

The police arrested Donald Halloway at 2:15 that afternoon.

Halloway was fifty-eight, an ex-coach from Ridgewood Prep whose wheelchair basketball program had been dismantled three years earlier amid allegations of recruiting violations and misuse of disability sport classifications—allegations that Ray Pulaski had reportedly helped surface. Halloway had never been formally charged with anything, but the whisper network of adaptive sports was small and permanent, and he'd been frozen out of coaching at every level. He'd been seen at an Eastlake game two weeks ago, sitting alone in the visitor section, staring down at the court with an expression that three separate witnesses would later describe, independently, as "murderous."

He was found at his apartment north of the city, sitting in a recliner, drinking a tallboy of Hamm's, watching *Judge Judy* with the volume up. When the detectives told him Ray Pulaski was dead, he smiled. It was a terrible smile. The detectives noted this.

"Couldn't have happened to a nicer guy," Halloway said.

Then: "You want to know if I did it?"

Then: "Sure. Yeah. Let's say I did."

He confessed in a rambling, forty-minute interview that the detectives would later describe as "forthcoming" and that Dez Okafor, watching it through a freedom-of-information request she shouldn't have been able to file for another two years, would describe as "a performance by a man who'd been waiting three years for someone to put him out of his misery."

The confession made the local news by six. The school released a statement by seven. By eight, the Eastlake Wheelhawks were gathered in the auxiliary gym—the main gym was taped off, a wound the school had papered over with a locked door and a printout that read CLOSED FOR MAINTENANCE—and interim head coach Erin Sugimoto was telling them that grief counselors would be available, that practice was cancelled until Friday, and that the Class 3A State Championship game, scheduled for Saturday at noon, was still on.

"Ray would've wanted you to play," Coach Sugimoto said, and she believed this, and she was right, and it didn't matter.

---

## Chapter 2

What the omniscient eye sees, hovering above the auxiliary gym at 8:16 p.m. on this Wednesday in December, is a circle of seven wheelchairs and the seven teenagers sitting in them, plus one woman standing with her arms crossed and her whistle hanging like a pendulum that has forgotten how to swing.

They are:

**Desirée "Dez" Okafor**, point guard, team captain, seventeen years old, spinal cord injury at T-10 sustained in a car accident at age nine. Four-point player in the International Wheelchair Basketball Federation classification system. Except that she isn't. What Dez knows—what she has known for four months, since Ray Pulaski pulled her aside after an August practice and said, *Chief, we need to talk about your classification card*—is that her functional ability was assessed at 3.5 during a classification camp in Indianapolis when she was fourteen, and that the 4.0 on file with the state athletic commission is the result of a form that was altered before submission. She did not alter it herself. She does not know who did. But she knows that Ray knew, and that Ray had given her until November 1st to come forward, and that November 1st had passed, and now November and most of December had passed, and Ray was dead, and the form was still on file, and her stomach had been a clenched fist for one hundred and nineteen days.

A wheelchair basketball team can field five players whose classification points total no more than 14.0. At 4.0, Dez is valued as a player with relatively high functional ability. At 3.5, she'd force the team's lineup math to change in ways that might cost them their championship-eligible roster. Or she'd force someone else off the court.

She found the body. She made the call. She has not yet told anyone about the classification card, and the omniscient eye watches her hold this knowledge like a coal against her chest—burning, yes, but if she opens her hands, everyone will see the light.

**Tomás Reyes**, center, sixteen years old, bilateral above-knee amputee since birth, 1.0-point player, six-foot-two in his chair and six-foot-five in the estimation of anyone who's tried to shoot over him. Profoundly deaf from age four—meningitis—and a lip-reader of startling, almost forensic precision. What Tomás knows is this: on Monday evening, two days before the murder, he was in the hallway outside Ray's office, waiting to pick up a replacement axle for his game chair, and he saw Ray through the office window, on the phone. Ray's back was mostly to the door. Mostly. But Tomás can read lips at a thirty-degree angle when the light is right, and the light was right, and Ray was saying: *I'm done covering for you, Erin. You tell them or I tell them, and I'm telling them Friday.*

Erin. Coach Erin Sugimoto. *Done covering.* Tomás has been turning these words over for two days with the frantic, silent intensity of a boy who has been taught, by a lifetime of being talked around and talked over, that the things you see when no one thinks you're watching are the things that will save your life or ruin it. He has told no one. He does not intend to. Coach Sugimoto is the person who fought the school board to keep the adaptive sports program funded. If she goes down, the Wheelhawks go with her.

**Keesha Williams**, shooting guard, seventeen years old, spina bifida, 2.0-point player, and the most technically perfect free-throw shooter in the state's adaptive division—74.3 percent from the line, a number she knows to the decimal because her mother, Patricia Williams, is a medical records administrator at St. Luke's Regional, and Patricia raised her daughter to believe that every meaningful truth eventually becomes a number in a file. What Keesha knows is clinical and damning: her mother mentioned, over reheated lasagna on Tuesday night, that Ray Pulaski had come into St. Luke's three weeks ago for an outpatient procedure and had, while there, requested copies of his own medical records going back ten years. Patricia had found this unremarkable. Keesha had not. People don't audit their own histories unless they're preparing for something—a lawsuit, an insurance claim, a confrontation. Keesha has not yet connected this to anything larger, but the thread is in her hand, and she can feel it humming.

She also knows—and this she holds closer—that her mother's access to hospital records is a door she has opened before, quietly, for purposes a medical records administrator should not permit. Keesha has never asked for details. She has benefited from the silence.

**Lina Choi**, bench player, fifteen years old, cerebral palsy primarily affecting her lower extremities, 2.5-point player, averaging four minutes of game time per contest, a fact that has made her functionally invisible to everyone in the Eastlake adaptive sports world except Ray Pulaski, who once told her, *Chief, the bench is the best seat in the house if you know what you're watching.* Lina knows the location of every unlocked door, every blind spot in the security camera system, every faculty bathroom with a lock that doesn't catch, because when you spend most of your life on the sideline, you learn the architecture of overlooked spaces. She's been inside the equipment cage after hours. She's been in the athletic director's filing cabinet. She's read things she should not have read, not out of malice but out of the same quiet, compulsive need that drives a wallflower to memorize every face at the party: if you can't be in the game, you can at least know everything about it.

What Lina knows, specifically, is that three weeks ago she found a folder in the equipment cage labeled CLASSIFICATION REVIEW - CONFIDENTIAL, and inside it were handwritten notes in Ray's cramped, slanting print, referencing four players across three schools—including Dez.

She has said nothing. She adores Dez. She would set herself on fire for Dez. This is not a metaphor she uses lightly; Lina has thought, with the rigor of someone who plans for every contingency, about what it would cost to destroy that folder, and she has decided the cost is acceptable, and she has not yet had the chance to go back for it because the gym is now a crime scene.

The other three players—**Marcus Webb**, power forward, grinning and anxious; **Jordyn Trask**, forward, who has already cried twice and is preparing to cry a third time; and **Aaliyah Montgomery**, reserve guard, silent, watchful, recording everything in the Notes app on her phone—are important because they are here. A team is not its stars. A team is the full bench, the last name on the roster, the body that shows up when showing up is the whole point.

And **Coach Erin Sugimoto**, standing, arms crossed, whistle still, who is thinking about Friday, and about what Ray Pulaski was going to say on Friday, and about whether dead men keep their deadlines.

---

## Chapter 3

The circle broke apart at 8:40, Coach Sugimoto heading for the parking lot with her keys already in her hand, Marcus and Jordyn wheeling toward the elevator that led to the dormitory wing, Aaliyah lingering with her phone like a girl waiting for a signal to move in a direction she hadn't chosen yet.

Dez said, "Stay."

She said it to Tomás first, then to Keesha, then to Lina. Not to the others. There was something surgical about her selections, and Aaliyah, watching from the doorway, felt the cut—but she left, because Aaliyah Montgomery was the kind of person who trusted that exclusion had a reason, even when the reason wasn't hers.

The auxiliary gym was smaller than the main gym but still vast enough that whispers died before they reached the walls. Dez wheeled to the center circle, the Eastlake hawk logo faded under her tires, and the other three followed, arranging themselves in a loose diamond: Keesha at her left wing, Lina slightly behind, Tomás directly across, watching her mouth with the patience of a boy who had learned years ago that most of what people said was filler and you needed only the bones.

"It wasn't Halloway," Dez said.

Keesha looked at her. "He confessed."

"He confessed to being glad Ray's dead. That's not the same thing."

"He literally told the cops he did it, Dez."

"He told the cops, 'Let's say I did.' I watched the interview."

A silence. Tomás's eyes moved between them. He read Keesha's doubt, the downward flicker of her lips. He read Dez's jaw, set like a latch on a door.

"How did you watch the interview?" Lina asked.

This was the thing about Lina: she found the detail that everyone else stepped over. Dez looked at her.

"I filed a public records request."

"You're sixteen."

"I filed it through the Eastlake Investigative Journalism Club account. I'm the only member."

Keesha let out a sound that was either a laugh or the ghost of one. "You're unreal."

"He didn't do it," Dez said again. She said it with the certainty of a mathematician, the kind that comes from having worked the proof backward and found the axiom cracked. "The timeline is wrong. Halloway's E-ZPass pinged a toll booth sixty-two miles north of here at 11:47 p.m. Tuesday. The M.E.'s preliminary window is between eleven and one a.m. Wednesday. That toll booth is a fifty-eight-minute drive from Eastlake in zero traffic.
